children.html: Associations Between Women's Body Image and Happiness: Results of the YouBeauty.com Body Image Survey (YBIS)
Viren Swami · Ulrich S. Tran · Stefan Stieger · Martin Voracek · The YouBeauty.com Team

Abstract Studies that have examined associations between body image and well-being have used limited measures of the former or have utilised small convenience samples. Here, we report on data from 9,667 Western women (US residents n = 8,925, non-US residents n = 742) who completed the online YouBeauty Body Image Survey. Respondents completed measures of weight-based body dissatisfaction, body appreciation, and subjective happiness, and provided demographic data including their education, age, and body mass index (BMI). Preliminary analyses indicated that 89.0 % of women evidenced weight-based body dissatisfaction, with the majority (84.1 %) wanting to be thinner. Path analysis showed that body appreciation positively predicted subjective happiness. BMI was negatively associated with body appreciation, but showed a direct positive association associated with subjective happiness. Controlling for BMI, body dissatisfaction had no significant association with subjective happiness. In addition, older and non-US respondents had higher body appreciation. Implications of the present results for intervention studies aimed at promoting healthier body image are discussed in conclusion.

In most socioeconomically developed settings, a strong message is sent to women that their physical appearance is of paramount importance and that the feminine ideal requires constant work on the body (Ahern et al. 2011; Swami and Smith 2012). These societal pressures often have detrimental effects on women's body image, which refers to a multidimensional construct comprising an individual's perceptions of, and attitudes toward, their bodies and physical appearance (Cash and Smolak 2011). Indeed, negative body image is now widely recognised as an important public health concern because of its increasing incidence worldwide. Although prevalence estimates have been problematised (Cash et al. 2004b), it is clear that a sizeable percentage of women experience negative body image of some form (Cash and Smolak 2011; Neighbors et al. 2008; Rozin et al. 2001; Pruis and Janowsky 2010). Moreover, there appear to be few differences in the experience of negative body image between women in different national settings worldwide (Swami et al. 2010). Such findings have led some scholars to suggest that negative body image is now a 'normative' experience in the lives of many women (Cash and Smolak 2011; Rodin et al. 1984).

Negative feelings, thoughts, and perceptions of one's body are of especial concern for several reasons. First, negative body image has been reliably linked with a range of disordered eating and weight-related outcomes, including frequent dieting (Ackard et al. 2002; Neumark-Sztainer et al. 2006a), bulimic symptoms and dietary restraint (Neumark-Sztainer et al. 2006b), and weight gain (van den Berg and Neumark-Sztainer 2007). Conversely, greater satisfaction with one's body has been shown to be associated with more positive health behaviours, including fruit and vegetable consumption (Ba and Kiziltan 2007) and engagement with physical activity (Kruger et al. 2008). Second, negative body image has been shown to be associated with poorer psychological well-being more generally (Keery et al. 2004), particularly symptoms of depression (Paxton et al. 2006), depressive mood (Mond et al. 2011), and lower self-esteem (Wertheim et al. 2001; van den Berg et al. 2010). It has been suggested that these negative effects occur partly because body image and corporeal experiences more generally are so highly embedded in women's live (Cash et al. 2004a; Lewis and Donaghue 2005).

Although this literature appears fairly conclusive, there are several important areas that require greater scholarly attention. First, studies that have assessed associations between body image and well-being have typically operationalised the former in terms of weightrelated constructs (e.g., perceptual differences between ideal and current body weight). While it is clear that dissatisfaction with one's weight is an important aspect of negative body image, it is also apparent that body image is a multidimensional construct that goes beyond weight (Cash and Smolak 2011). Thus, by choosing to focus on weight-related constructs, scholars may be missing other important aspects of body image that have an impact on women's well-being. This limitation of extant studies may be overcome by operationalising evaluative body image more broadly.

For example, a number of scholars have recently emphasised the importance of examining positive, adaptive, or healthy body image (Avalos et al. 2005; Smolak and Cash 2011). Indeed, qualitative studies have highlighted the value of positive body attitudes, such as body appreciation, body acceptance, and functional corporeal orientation, when discussing women's bodily experiences (Frise´n and Holmqvist 2010; Wood-Barcalow

et al. 2010). In particular, body appreciation (that is, a tendency to hold favourable opinions of one's body regardless of its appearance, acceptance and respect of the body and its needs, and protection of the body from unrealistic ideals) has been shown to be positively associated with women's self-esteem, optimism, and sexual satisfaction (Satinsky et al. 2012; Swami et al. 2008a, b) and negatively with disturbed body attitudes and eating disorder symptomatology (Augustus-Horvath and Tylka 2011; Iannantuono and Tylka 2012; Swami et al. 2013). More generally, focusing on body appreciation fits with the call in the social sciences to change the focus from dealing with negative outcomes to promoting positive qualities as a method of prevention (Seligman and Csikszentmihalyi 2000). Studying associations between positive body image and well-being could, therefore, aid scholars in understanding both how to prevent body image disturbance as well as uncovering protective factors.

Secondly, studies that have examined associations between negative body image and wellbeing have tended to adopt relatively constricted definitions of the latter, typically focusing on self-esteem. However, it is also apparent that women's body image contributes to more comprehensive quality of life and well-being attitudes (Diener et al. 1995; Donaghue 2009). Thus, for example, several studies have reported that women's body image (variously measured as body esteem, body dissatisfaction, and self-reported physical attractiveness) is associated with their life satisfaction, a measure of subjective well-being (Diener et al. 1995; Donaghue 2009; Stokes and Frederick-Recascino 2003). That is, women's satisfaction with life appears to be influenced by their corporeal attitudes and embodied aspects of the self, distinct from their feelings of self-worth (Frederickson et al. 1998).

In addition to life satisfaction, subjective well-being can also be approached at a more 'molar' or global level by assessing an individual's summary assessment of their subjective happiness (Lyubomirsky and Lepper 1999). In this view, subjective happiness is thought to tap more global psychological phenomena compared with measures of life satisfaction (i.e., beyond recent levels of affect and specific satisfaction with life) and allows for an assessment of the extent to which an individual is a happy or unhappy person. That is, while life satisfaction is an important component of subjective well-being, it can be distinguished conceptually from subjective happiness (Bartels and Boomsma 2009; Mattei and Schaeder 2004), which is a more affective state and less consistent over time (Moons et al. 2006). Moreover, to our knowledge, no previous study has examined associations between women's body image and subjective happiness.

Another issue that warrants further investigation is the relationships between age, socioeconomic status (SES), and women's body image. In the first instance, it is known that women's bodies across the lifespan are affected by ageing, childbirth, dietary changes, hormonal fluctuations, and changes in physical activity (Slevec and Tiggemann 2011; Peat et al. 2008; Tiggemann and Lynch 2001), which in turn may have an impact on body image. For instance, the increase in body mass index (BMI) through middle age (Sheehan et al. 2003) may widen perceived discrepancies between current and ideal body sizes.

Concurrently, however, objectification pressures may decline with age (Tiggemann and Lynch 2001) and older women may also develop resources that focus attention on the body's functionality rather than appearance (Avalos et al. 2005). Not surprisingly, when large-sample studies have examined associations between women's weight-related body dissatisfaction, they have returned equivocal results, with some studies indicating that negative body image increases with age (Frederick et al. 2006; Swami et al. 2010) and others reporting no significant association (Runfola et al. 2013). These mixed findings necessitate a closer examination of associations between age and body image.

In addition, few studies have investigated relationships between body image and SES status among Western women, although it has been reported in at least one non-Western context that low SES women have more positive body image than their high SES counterparts. Among Western girls and women, large-scale studies have suggests that there may not be significant associations between measures of body image and SES (e.g., Story et al. 1995; Swami et al. 2010; van den Berg et al. 2010). However, other studies have suggested that weight issues, dietary restraint, attempts to lose weight, and poor body esteem may be higher among women of higher SES (e.g., O'Dea and Caputi 2001; Walters and Kendler 1995). In the present study, therefore, we included a measure of educational status as a general proxy for respondent SES.

In the present study, we examined associations between women's body image and subjective happiness using data from the YouBeauty.com Body Image Survey (YBIS). More specifically, respondents from the West (primarily the United States) completed two measures of body image, namely weight-related body dissatisfaction (actual-ideal weight discrepancy) and body appreciation. We further examined the impact of respondent age and education on the associations between body image and subjective happiness. We proposed a hypothesised model, derived from the above review of the extant literature, in which education and age shape respondent BMI, which in turn affect body dissatisfaction and body appreciation. The latter two variables were predicted to affect subjective happiness in opposite directions (see Fig. 1).

The total sample initially comprised 14,056 participants who completed the YBIS between September and December 2012, of whom 11,321 were US residents and 2,735 were non-US residents. Following ethical stipulations, we excluded from analyses participants who were under 18 years of age (n = 3,058). Furthermore, we only used participants who provided complete datasets with regard to the hypothesized model, leaving 8,925 US residents and 1,900 non-US residents. We further checked whether participants reported implausible BMIs, operationalised as <7 \text{ kg/m}^2 \text{ or } > 60 \text{ kg/m}^2 (Young et al. 2001), but all respondent BMIs ranged between 10.13 and 44.98 kg/m². Non-US residents originated from 135 different countries (113 participants did not provide information about their country of residence). Of these participants, only three countries provided participants above a 5 % threshold, namely Canada (22.0 %), United Kingdom (14.2 %), and Australia (5.3 %). We, therefore, limited our analyses in the non-US sample to residents of these three countries. Therefore, the final datasets comprised 8,925 US residents and 742 non-US residents. Characteristics of the final samples are reported in Table 1.

To measure actual-ideal weight discrepancy, we used the Photographic Figure Rating Scale (Swami et al. 2008c), a figural rating scale in which participants are presented with 10 photographic images of women ranging in body size from emaciated to obese. All images were presented in greyscale, with faces obscured, in standard clothing, and in front-view. As with all figural rating scales, participants were asked to rate (in this case, using dropdown menus) the figure that most closely matched their own body and the figure that they would most likely to possess. Ratings were made on a 10-point scale (1 = Figure \ with \ the \ lowest \ BMI, 10 = Figure \ with \ the \ highest \ BMI). For the purposes of analyses, we

operationalised body dissatisfaction as the difference between unsigned (absolute) current and ideal ratings, which is consistent with the way this variable is computed in previous studies (Swami and Harris 2012; Swami and Tove´e 2009). Previous studies have shown that scores derived from this measure have good patterns of validity and good test–retest reliability up to 5 weeks (Swami et al. 2011b, 2012, 2013).

Body appreciation was measured using the Body Appreciation Scale (Avalos et al. 2005), a 13-item scale that measures related dimensions of positive body image. All items were rated on a 5-point Likert-type scale (1 = Never, 5 = Always) and an overall score was computed as the mean of all items (higher scores on this scale represent higher body appreciation). This scale has been shown to have a one-dimensional factor structure among women from Western settings (Avalos et al. 2005; Swami et al. 2008d). Among non-Western women, however, the scale's one-dimensional factor structure has not been replicated (Swami and Chamorro-Premuzic 2008; Swami et al. 2011a; Swami and Jaafar 2012), providing further reason to omit non-Western women from our sample. The scale has also been shown to have good test–retest reliability over a 3-week period (Avalos et al. 2005) and has good patterns of construct and discriminant validity with college and community samples (Avalos et al. 2005; Swami et al. 2008b). In the present study, Cronbach's alphas for this scale were .92 for both US and non-US residents.

Participants completed the Subjective Happiness Scale (Lyubomirsky and Lepper 1999), a 4-item scale with a 7-point Likert-type response scale. On two items of the scale, participants characterise themselves based on absolute ratings (1 = Not a very happy person, 7 = A very happy person) and relative to peers (1 = Less happy, 7 = More happy), while on two further items they rate the extent to which descriptions of happy and unhappy persons are characteristic of themselves (1 = Not at all, 7 = A great deal). An overall score of subjective happiness is computed as the mean of all items, following reversecoding of one item. Higher scores on this scale reflect greater subjective happiness. The scale has been shown to have good patterns of convergent and divergent validity and test– retest reliability up to 1 year (Lyubomirsky and Lepper 1999; Swami 2008; Swami et al. 2009). Internal consistency coefficients for this scale were good for both the US and non-US samples (Cronbach's alpha in both cases = .89).

Participants self-reported their height and weight, which we used to calculate their BMI as kg/m2 . Self-reported height and weight data have been shown to be very strongly correlated with measured data and are valid for identifying relationships in population studies (Spencer et al. 2002).
Participants self-reported their age and were asked to confirm that they were female. Participants were also requested to self-report their highest educational qualification,

ethnicity, and country of residence using predetermined drop-down menus. Educational categories included the following: (1) Some high school; (2) High school diploma or equivalent; (3) Some college; (4) Undergraduate degree; (5) Graduate degree.

The study was approved by the relevant university ethics committee and all participants provided informed consent online. Data were derived from the YBIS, an online crosssectional survey hosted at the health and beauty website YouBeauty.com between September and December 2012. The survey was advertised on the parent site and potential participants who visited the site were invited to complete the YBIS, which was linked to from the main webpage. Additionally, potential participants could access the survey via a separate quiz page hosted by the parent site. The survey was presented across seven webpages, the first of which invited participation in a survey on body image and mood. The second page presented a disclaimer in which participants were presented with their ethical rights and further information about the lead investigator. Providing informed consent began the survey on a new page with items of the Body Appreciation Scale. Subsequent pages presented items from the Subjective Happiness Scale, the Photographic Figure Rating Scale, and a scale not utilised here, while the penultimate page requested demographic information. The final page provided participants with personalised feedback on their body image and subjective happiness. Participation in the survey was voluntary and participants were not remunerated for completing the survey.

Analysis proceeded in three steps. First, the fit of the hypothesised model (see Fig. 1) was investigated in the larger US sample. Education and age were entered as exogenous variables with direct paths to the mediating variables of BMI, body appreciation, and body dissatisfaction. Body appreciation and body dissatisfaction were allowed to correlate in this model (not shown in Fig. 1). While BMI was allowed to mediate the effects of education and age on body appreciation and body dissatisfaction, it was only the two latter variables that were hypothesised to possess direct paths to subjective happiness. Second, the model was improved by adding additional paths, guided by modification indices (see Fig. 2). Third, the final model was fit to the data of both the US and the smaller non-US sample using multi-group analysis, allowing us to test whether fit was satisfactory across the samples and whether path coefficients were of comparable size.

Mplus 6.11 (Muthe´n and Muthe´n 2008) was used for path analyses, using estimation methods (mean- and variance-corrected maximum likelihood estimation) that provide robust standard errors and robust tests of model fit. For the evaluation of model fit, the comparative fit index (CFI), the Tucker–Lewis index (TLI), and the root mean square error of approximation (RMSEA) with 90 % confidence interval were used. For a good fit, standard benchmarks (Hu and Bentler 1999) were utilized (CFI and TLI: C.95; RMSEA: \.06).

Furthermore, the proportion with higher educational levels was higher in the non-US than in the US sample, v2 (4) = 67.01, p\.001. There were no significant differences between US and non-US residents in body appreciation, t(9,665) = 1.59, p = .112, d = .06. Compared with the non-US sample, the US sample had significantly higher body dissatisfaction, t(9,665) = 2.45, p = .014, d = .09, and subjective happiness, t(9,665) = 3.73, p\.001, d = .14, although effect sizes were small and negligible. With regard to the body dissatisfaction data, 89.0 % of participants reported some discrepancy (=0) between their ideal and their actual body shape: 84.1 % wanted to be thinner and only 4.9 % larger. There were no significant differences in these proportions between the US and non-US samples, v2 (2) = 4.95, p = .084 (note that, for the purposes of subsequent analyses, body dissatisfaction scores were computed as unsigned data).

Fit of the hypothesised model (Fig. 1) was acceptable in the US sample, \chi^2 = 291.41, df = 7, p < .001, CFI = .969, TLI = .939, RMSEA = .067 [.061, .074]. Coefficients of all hypothesised paths were significant. However, the effects of education on BMI and of body dissatisfaction on subjective happiness were small (standardized path coefficients \leq 1.081). Importantly, controlling for body appreciation, the path coefficient of body dissatisfaction to subjective well-being was positive, despite its small size. Modification indices suggested additional paths from age to body appreciation, and from BMI to subjective happiness. This modified model (see Fig. 2) had a very good fit on the data of the US sample, \chi^2 = 57.51, df = 5, p < .001, CFI = .994, TLI = .984, RMSEA = .034 [.027, .043] and also in the multi-group analysis, \chi^2 = 74.01, df = 10, p < .001, CFI = .993, TLI = .981, RMSEA = .036 [.029, .044]. Path coefficients were nearly identical across the two samples. Constraining all coefficients to identity across the two samples, we again found a good model fit, \chi^2 = 89.64, df = 19, p < .001, CFI = .993, TLI = .989, RMSEA = .028 [.022, .034]. Standardized path coefficients of this multigroup model are displayed in Fig. 2 (note that unstandardised coefficients were constrained; standardised coefficients differed somewhat between the samples because of slight differences of dispersion). All path coefficients were highly significant (p < .001), with exception of body dissatisfaction on subjective happiness (ps = .295 in the two samples).

The exogenous variables explained 4.3 and 4.9 % of BMI in the US and non-US samples, whereas exogenous variables and BMI explained 6.2 and 4.7 %, respectively, of body appreciation scores, and 29.9 and 24.1 %, respectively, of body dissatisfaction scores. BMI and body appreciation scores in turn explained 28.9 and 27.8 %, respectively, of subjective happiness scores. Older age was associated with a higher body appreciation and higher BMI in both samples, lower educational levels with a higher BMI. Body appreciation showed a strong and positive association with subjective happiness. The association of BMI with subjective happiness was more complex: overall, a higher BMI had a direct negative effect on body appreciation and thus an indirect negative effect on subjective happiness. This indirect effect had standardized coefficients of -.13 and -.11 (ps < .001), respectively, in the two samples. However, a higher BMI also had a slight but consistent direct positive effect on subjective happiness. Taken together, the total effect of BMI on subjective happiness was negative and had a size of only -.04 in both samples (ps < .001). Body dissatisfaction was strongly positively associated with BMI. However, controlling for BMI, body dissatisfaction had no significant association with subjective happiness.

Using data from the YBIS, we examined the relationships between body image and subjective happiness in two samples of Western women. Overall, our results indicated that women's body appreciation is a strong positive predictor of their subjective happiness. In turn, body appreciation was associated with respondent age and BMI. The latter variable showed a more complex relationship with subjective happiness: BMI had a direct and positive association with subjective happiness, but was also negatively associated with body appreciation. In short, it might be concluded that women who have more positive body attitudes experience greater global happiness, while body appreciation in turn is influenced by a complex set of factors.
The association between body appreciation and happiness generally corroborates previous work indicating that the former predicts indices of well-being among women (Wood-

Barcalow et al. 2010; Satinsky et al. 2012; Swami et al. 2008a, b). It is also consistent with reports that women's body image more broadly contribute to their well-being (Diener et al. 1995; Donaghue 2009; Stokes and Frederick-Recascino 2003). Importantly, however, our results indicated that body appreciation might have stronger associations with subjective happiness than weight-based body dissatisfaction. For example, the direct relationship between body appreciation and subjective happiness in our hypothesised model was .57, whereas that of body dissatisfaction and subjective happiness was positive and only .06. It might be suggested that body appreciation, as a more global measure of body image, is highly correlated with a generalised sense of well-being or self-esteem (Roberts et al. 2006), which is driving the present set of results. However, taken at face value, our results also highlight the strong coupling between women's corporeal attitudes and their overall well-being (Ahern et al. 2011).

Just as important, the present findings may highlight important avenues for intervention. Thus, while the bulk of interventionist programmes seeks to ameliorate the negative outcomes of body dissatisfaction, focusing on body appreciation may allow practitioners to highlight the importance of positive qualities (Tylka 2011). For example, therapists might promote improved body appreciation by aiding their clients to respect and appreciate their bodies, teaching them to focus on the body's functionality rather than appearance, becoming mindful of the body's needs, and rejecting critical messages (e.g., from the media; Iannantuono and Tylka 2012; Tylka 2011). That is, while we do not dispute the importance of attending to body dissatisfaction, our results also suggest that promoting respect for, and acceptance of, the body may be a more direct means of promoting positive body image among women.

It is important to note, however, that both our body image variables were themselves shaped by a number of difference factors, including age and BMI. In terms of age, for example, we found that both body dissatisfaction and body appreciation increased with older age. It is possible that, as women age, they develop greater respect for the body and focus on its functionality (Avalos et al. 2005); an increase in body mass with age, however, may also mean that older women experience a greater discrepancy between their current body size and perceived or societal ideals (Swami et al. 2010). In addition, we found that women of lower SES (as measured using the proxy of education) had higher BMIs, which is consistent with previous work (van den Berg et al. 2010), although it would be useful for future work to utilise better measures of SES.

One other result from our survey was noteworthy. Examining body dissatisfaction specifically, it was apparent that 89.0 % of women in our survey experienced some form of weight-based dissatisfaction, with the vast majority wanting to be thinner. This finding is consistent with recent work (Runfola et al. 2013) indicating that about 91.0 % of women evidence a discrepancy between their current and ideal body sizes. Although limited to weight-based body dissatisfaction, the high percentage of women who want to be thinner warrants attention, as it highlights the ubiquity of the thin ideal in most contemporary societies (Swami et al. 2010). In addition, the moderate negative association between body dissatisfaction and body appreciation highlights the complex link between these different aspects of body image. Attempts to promote healthier body image by promoting body appreciation should not neglect to tackle the thin ideal and its deleterious consequences.

Our findings should be considered in light of several limitations. First, because our samples were self-selecting, they should not be considered representative of wider populations. Furthermore, because our survey was conducted online, our sample may be biased toward women with Internet access, who are more affluent (United States Census Bureau 2009), or women who have a higher concern with weight or appearance. Second, our aim

of recruiting a large sample necessitated a relatively brief survey; this, in turn, meant that we neglected other potentially important variables that may have mediated associations that we reported on. Such variables include general well-being indices such as self-esteem, demographic variables such as ethnicity, as well as corporeal-related constructs such as internalisation of the thin ideal and appearance-orientation.

Third, the accuracy of self-reported data cannot be established in the present instance. For example, although self-reported height and weight are strongly correlated with objectively measured data, there is also a tendency among women to over-report height and under-report their weight (Engstrom et al. 2003). In a similar vein, although our use of education as a proxy for SES is consistent with previous studies that have used education or measures derived from educational qualifications (e.g., van den Berg et al. 2010), future studies may wish to utilise more (cross-culturally) valid and reliable measures of SES. Finally, the cross-sectional nature of our study means that, although we have interpreted our data consistent with previous studies, we cannot ascertain the direction of predictive associations with certainty. Longitudinal studies will be required to analyse the ways in which body image affects subjective happiness, or vice versa.

In conclusion, the present results suggest that body dissatisfaction, as measured by weight-based discrepancy between current and ideal body sizes, may be fairly ubiquitous among Western women. However, our results also highlight the important role played by body appreciation in enhancing subjective happiness. Women who hold more favourable opinions of their body, who accept and respect their bodies, and who protect their bodies from unrealistic ideals appear to be happier than women who have lower body appreciation. Certainly, further quantitative and qualitative studies are required to ascertain the way in which body image impacts upon women's well-being. In the meantime, however, teaching women how to develop more positive body appreciation may provide a means of tackling the global body image problem.
